transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-01-15
Start time: 16:30 PST
Duration: ~65 minutes
Attendees: Evan Park (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Luca Fernandez (Redwood Platform), Maya Chen (Lead ML Eng, Crestline), Ravi Patel (Infra Architect), Sofia Martinez (Security), Tom Briggs (SRE)

Auto-summary: quick technical deep dive; mostly SE-to-SE; some security questions. Call ended with concrete pilot next steps.

[00:00] Evan Park: ok hey everyone, thanks for carving time. we promised a focused review of caching strategy — specifically prefix/prompt caching, hit-rates, and how to keep multi-tenant safety. i think priya has a short diagram she wants to walk through.
[00:18] Priya Shah: yeah hi all, i'll share my screen in a sec. the main things we want to land: how you compute cache keys, where you apply tenant isolation, and what the runtime does when collisions or TTLs hit. i'll call out a couple of patterns: logical namespacing, hash-salting per-tenant, and physical siloing (dedicated cache per tenant).
[00:36] Maya Chen: sounds good, appreciate it. quick context: our product generates clinical triage summaries; prompts are templated but we have lots of subtle variants per customer config. we care a lot about hitting latency SLAs and also can't leak patient PII between tenants.
[00:52] Ravi Patel: and from infra side we have strict network egress rules, and for enterprise customers some want on-prem or VPC-only deployments with HSM for keys.
[01:08] Priya Shah: that's helpful. ok first slide: cache-key anatomy. naive key is full prompt text + model + model-params (temperature, top_p). we usually normalize whitespace, canonicalize placeholders, and optionally strip high-entropy inputs (PHI). we then hash the normalized prompt + model-id + tenant-id(optional) + quantization-profile -> 256-bit digest.
[01:30] Tom Briggs: two quick Qs: do you include tenant-id in the hash or use a namespace prefix? there's an operational difference when using shared caches across tenants.
[01:45] Luca Fernandez: good point. we typically recommend either a) prefixing keys with tenant-id when using a shared cache, or b) omitting tenant-id in environments where the cache is physically siloed per-tenant (e.g., dedicated Redis instance per tenant). prefixing gives strong logical isolation but adds risk if tenant-ids are guessable and you have multi-tenant cache exposure — though guessability isn't a big issue if you never expose cache endpoints externally.
[02:10] Sofia Martinez: from security perspective we want defense-in-depth. prefixing plus per-tenant HMAC using tenant-secret is an option so a rogue process can't enumerate keys. is HMAC supported?
[02:26] Priya Shah: yes, runtime supports optional HMAC-salting. we can derive a per-tenant secret (either from your KMS/HSM or Redwood-managed token) and include it in the key derivation. that prevents enumeration and accidental cross-tenant lookups. there is a small CPU overhead at key creation time but negligible compared to token generation costs.
[02:46] Maya Chen: what about prompts that include dynamic user data — like patient notes — should we strip that out before hashing so the cache can match more generally?
[02:58] Priya Shah: we recommend separating stable template portions from user-specific slots. cache keys should be built from the template + canonicalized slot signatures (e.g., slot-types like "PHI_TEXT" instead of the full content). for some flows you can also store short fingerprint of the dynamic content to validate freshness without including the full content.
[03:22] Ravi Patel: interesting — so we could get higher hit rates by normalizing. do you have numbers on how much hit-rate improves?
[03:31] Evan Park: we find normalization and slotting can improve effective hit-rate 2x-5x depending on variance. in early pilots with templated prompts for support chat, hit-rates jumped from ~8% to ~38% after canonicalization. clinical flows are noisier but the same techniques hold.
[03:52] Tom Briggs: ok eviction — how do you set TTLs? we have bursty traffic and don't want cache thrashing.
[04:02] Priya Shah: TTL is workload dependent. patterns we recommend: short TTL (30s-2m) for interactive chat where freshness is critical, longer TTL (5-60m) for completions with templated prompts. combine LRU with frequency decays: keep hot keys longer, evict cold ones quickly. also consider size-based eviction for prefix caches: store fingerprints for large keys and full outputs for small ones.
[04:28] Maya Chen: any built-in metrics we should capture during the pilot to measure effectiveness?
[04:35] Priya Shah: yes: key insertion rate, hit-rate by template-id, cold-start rate, average latency delta (cache hit vs miss), and token-savings estimate. we'll provide an instrumentation script to emit these to your monitoring stack.
[04:50] [05:00] -- brief pause while Evan posts the instrumentation link in chat --
[05:10] Ravi Patel: talk to me about collisions — two different normalized prompts hashing to same digest. how often does that happen and what's the mitigation?
[05:22] Luca Fernandez: with a 256-bit hash collisions are astronomically unlikely in practice. operationally you'll see logical collisions from overzealous normalization — e.g., two templates normalized to same slot signature; that's an application-level collision. mitigation: keep template metadata in key (template-id) or store versioned value blobs with checksum. also make the key include model-params and quantization-profile so model-signature mismatches don't reuse an incompatible cached token sequence.
[05:52] Sofia Martinez: quantization profile — if you serve the same logical model but with different quantization (int8 vs int4), can you reuse outputs?
[06:03] Priya Shah: generally no — quantization can change output distribution subtly. we include quantization-profile in key-bytes. small quantization differences can change tokens especially in tail. for cost-conscious flows we support "compatible quantization families" where outputs are considered functionally equivalent, but that's a configurable policy and requires eval.
[06:26] Maya Chen: what about batching — if we batch requests together for throughput, does that change caching semantics?
[06:36] Priya Shah: batching is orthogonal. cache lookups are done pre-batch: we check each request, answer cache hits immediately, and only send misses to the batcher. batching helps throughput for misses but you still need fast cache lookup in the hot path. note: very large batch sizes can increase memory pressure and KV cache performance variance; we recommend workload-aware batching where queueing delays are bounded.
[07:00] Tom Briggs: we have strict PII rules. how do you ensure PHI isn't written to shared cache in hosted mode?
[07:11] Priya Shah: options: a) strip PHI at SDK layer and never cache those prompts, b) encrypt cached values at rest using tenant-specific keys (HSM-backed), or c) use private/dedicated caches per tenant. hosted mode offers tenant-encryption and HSM integration as an enterprise add-on; for highest assurance we recommend private deployment with your KMS.
[07:33] Sofia Martinez: encryption at rest is good but what about in-memory exposure on shared hosts?
[07:40] Luca Fernandez: in-memory is protected by process boundaries, but shared Redis clusters still have memory accessible to the process. dedicated instances avoid co-tenancy. additionally, we support token-level redaction and never store raw PHI in plaintext — we store deterministic fingerprints and encrypted blobs.
[07:58] Ravi Patel: can you walk through a sample cache-key example? show me concrete string composition.
[08:05] Priya Shah: sure. example: "tenant:crestline|tmpl:triage_v2|model:gptx-11b|qp:int8-r2|slots:SYM_3|hash:ab12...ef". if HMAC enabled the final stored key becomes "hmac_v1:zz34...". we avoid embedding whole prompt text in key to keep key sizes small.
[08:33] Maya Chen: that helps. another concern: multi-tenant safety with noisy neighbors — if Tenant A floods the cache with large unique prompts it can evict keys for Tenant B if you're using shared cache. what's recommended?
[08:46] Evan Park: for noisy neighbor protection, use either quota-based cache partitions (Redis maxmemory-policy with volatile-ttl scoped by tenant) or create physical sharding (many small Redis instances keyed by hash of tenant-id). Redwood Dedicated offers configurable cache pools with eviction reservations per-tenant.
[09:06] Tom Briggs: do you support tenant-level quotas out of the box or do we manage via infra?
[09:12] Priya Shah: we have controllers that can enforce cache quotas and monitor per-tenant eviction rates; they can surface alerts and automatically spin secondary cache for heavy tenants. this is part of Redwood Dedicated and can be added to Redwood Private with a bit of ops work.
[09:27] Maya Chen: curious about a hybrid approach — keep small templates in shared cache and heavy unstructured prompts in a per-tenant store. does that pattern work?
[09:36] Luca Fernandez: yes, that's a common hybrid. classify keys by size or template-stability. small, stable templates go to shared fast cache; large or sensitive content goes to tenant-specific stores or never cached. the runtime supports classification rules so you can implement this without changing call sites.
[09:51] [10:00] -- short ambient cross-talk as attendees nod --
[10:12] Sofia Martinez: compliance question: do you keep audit logs of cache hits? we need tractability for SOC2.
[10:20] Priya Shah: yes, audit events include cache lookups and cache misses with template-id and masked key fingerprint. we avoid logging raw prompt text in audit logs. logs are available in the Console and can be exported to your SIEM.
[10:34] Ravi Patel: for on-prem pilot: what footprint do you expect for our staging cluster? GPUs + redis size estimates?
[10:42] Evan Park: depends on QPS and model sizes. for a staging pilot with ~200 qps peak and a mid-size model (8-12B), plan for 1-2 A100-equivalent GPUs and ~200-500GB of Redis depending on retention and average output sizes. we'll send a sizing template.
[11:00] Maya Chen: re: pilot instrumentation, we want the script to tag keys with template-id and variant so we can correlate hit-rate by template. is that supported?
[11:10] Priya Shah: yep, instrumentation will emit template-id, normalized-key-hash, hit/miss, latency, and model-params. it'll be a small agent or a lightweight SDK wrapper.
[11:22] Tom Briggs: what's the expected hit-rate uplift if we also enable prefix prefetching?
[11:30] Priya Shah: prefetching can help for predictable flows (e.g., chat systems with suggested completions). we've seen another 10-25% uplift on top of normalization when prefix prefetching is safe. caveat: prefetching increases upstream load if predictions are wrong. it's best for bounded suggestion sets.
[11:50] Maya Chen: are there specific pitfalls you warn customers about? like over-normalizing and serving wrong content?
[11:58] Priya Shah: yes — over-normalization can collapse semantics. always preserve semantic tokens (e.g., user intent markers). have a small human-reviewed policy for normalization rules. also watch out for quantization mismatches and tokenization edge-cases — we recommend running an eval harness to detect regressions before enabling aggressive cross-tenant caching.
[12:18] Ravi Patel: ok last area: HSM/KMS integration for Redwood Private — how does key rotation work for HMAC salts used in cache keys?
[12:27] Luca Fernandez: we support key rotation via staged rollover. new keys are used for HMAC but we maintain a short-lived lookup table for previous keys so old entries remain addressable for their TTL. we also support double-write during rotation windows if you want zero-loss. we'll document the rotation flow once we map to your KMS.
[12:46] Sofia Martinez: do you store the HMAC secrets on Redwood side for hosted customers?
[12:51] Evan Park: by default Redwood-managed secrets are used in hosted mode; for enterprise we integrate with customer KMS/HSM so Redwood never sees plaintext.
[13:02] Maya Chen: ok great. i think we have actionable next steps. one quick question: can we run a small synthetic that simulates prompt variance? i.e., we can replay logs and measure hit-rate improvement with normalization heuristics.
[13:12] Priya Shah: absolutely — replay is our recommended first step. we'll provide the harness; you feed historical prompts, we run normalization + hashing offline and return simulated hit-rate and token-savings.
[13:26] Evan Park: perfect. last recap: Redwood sends key spec, instrumentation, and sizing template. Crestline runs staging replay and benchmark, returns hit-rates. we'll follow with on-prem scoping session for VPC/HSM concerns.
[13:41] Maya Chen: thanks everyone. that works.
[13:45] Evan Park: thanks all, we'll email a meeting notes + artifacts.
[13:50] [End of meeting]
